Avec CMD en forme exec (node server.js), le process reçoit le signal et s'arrête en 200 ms. Une ligne dans le Dockerfile, et les déploiements ne traînent plus.

comments.body: Pareil pour les requêtes en cours : sans arrêt propre elles sont coupées. Ajoute server.close() sur SIGTERM pour laisser finir ce qui est commencé avant de quitter.
server.close attend les connexions keep-alive encore ouvertes. Il faut aussi fermer les connexions inactives, closeIdleConnections existe depuis Node 18.2.
Oui, j'ai ajouté un délai de grâce de 8 secondes avant le process.exit final.
Docker a aussi l'option --init (tini) si tu ne veux pas toucher au code. Elle gère le signal et les processus zombies.
Tini règle le problème du PID 1, mais ton application doit quand même gérer SIGTERM pour finir proprement ses requêtes. Sinon elle est juste tuée plus gentiment.
8 secondes de grâce, c'est quoi le délai de ton orchestrateur ? Sous Compose, stop_grace_period est de 10 secondes par défaut, garde de la marge sinon le kill arrive pendant ton nettoyage.
Côté front, quand un déploiement coupait une requête, on voyait des 502 intermittents à chaque mise en production. C'était notre premier signe du problème, avant même qu'on regarde le Dockerfile.

title: tabledrift 0.2 : comparer une table du monolithe avec sa copie dans le service
body: tabledrift 0.2 est sorti. Petit outil en ligne de commande écrit en Java, qui compare une table PostgreSQL du monolithe avec la table équivalente du nouveau service : colonnes manquantes, types différents, valeurs par défaut et nombre de lignes. Je l'utilise pendant la migration, une table à la fois, pour savoir quand on peut basculer les lectures. Nouveau dans 0.2 : comparaison des clés primaires et des contraintes NOT NULL, sortie JSON pour la CI. Pas encore : les index, les clés étrangères et tout ce qui n'est pas PostgreSQL.

comments.body: Les index, c'est justement ce qui fait mal en production après une bascule : une requête qui passait en 5 ms parce qu'un index existait dans le monolithe et pas dans la copie. Je les mettrais avant les NOT NULL dans ta liste. Tu compares aussi le contenu ou seulement le nombre de lignes ?

body: Porting a Java Android screen to Flutter, I translated the old AsyncTask logic literally and ended up with five booleans for loading, refreshing, error, empty and has data, with combinations nobody could explain. Replaced them with a single state object with four cases and the screen went from 380 lines to 140. Should have started there instead of translating line by line.

comments.body: Same idea in pipeline code. A status field per record with explicit values beats several booleans, because the booleans eventually disagree and nobody knows which one to believe.
An explicit status per record, yes. We also store when it last changed, and the oldest items in each state show up on a dashboard. That is how we found rows stuck for weeks.
Did you keep the old Java screen running in parallel for a release? We ship the Flutter one behind a flag and compare crash rates for a week before removing the old one.

body: Jauge de remplissage des salles pendant le festival, rafraîchie toutes les 10 secondes. Aujourd'hui, un setInterval dans un useEffect. Je me demande si je passe à react-query avec refetchInterval, et comment arrêter le polling quand l'onglet est caché pour ne pas gaspiller la batterie et les données des gens. Qu'est-ce que vous utilisez ?

comments.body: Pourquoi pas du SSE ? Un flux du serveur vers le client, pas de requête toutes les 10 secondes pour rien. Nginx sait le servir, et React n'a besoin que d'un EventSource.
Derrière certains proxys d'opérateurs ou un CDN, le flux peut être mis en mémoire tampon et les mises à jour arrivent par paquets. On a fini par revenir au polling avec ETag.
Avec ETag, une réponse 304 ne pèse presque rien. Sur une connexion lente, c'est exactement ce qui compte. Le polling toutes les 10 secondes devient acceptable.

Le tampon vient souvent de Nginx lui-même : proxy_buffering off sur la route SSE, ou l'en-tête X-Accel-Buffering à no envoyé par l'application. Ça a réglé le problème chez nous, au moins derrière notre propre proxy.

react-query ne rafraîchit pas en arrière-plan par défaut : refetchIntervalInBackground est à false, donc le polling s'arrête tout seul quand l'onglet est caché. Pour un setInterval maison, regarde document.visibilityState.

body: Petite victoire sur le programme du festival : le premier affichage est passé de 2,8 s à 1,3 s sur un Samsung A03 avec la 3G limitée dans Chrome. Le changement : une seule graisse de la police web au lieu de quatre, avec font-display swap. Le reste du bundle n'a pas bougé. Parfois c'est la police et rien d'autre.

title: Keras and PyTorch disagree at 1e-3 because of one epsilon
body: Porting a Keras model to PyTorch for a shared scoring service, outputs differed by around 1e-3 on the same input. First cause: BatchNorm epsilon, 1e-3 in Keras and 1e-5 in PyTorch by default. Matching it brought the difference down to about 4e-5, but not to zero, and I am still looking. On 2,000 saved inputs, 0.7 percent of predictions at the 0.5 threshold flip between the two versions.

comments.body: Check stride 2 convolutions with same padding. TensorFlow pads asymmetrically when the size is odd, PyTorch pads symmetrically, so the windows are shifted by a pixel. That gave me exactly this kind of leftover difference.
That was it. Two stride 2 convs. Explicit padding before them took the difference down to 1e-6 and the flips went to zero on the 2,000 inputs.
How do you know 1e-3 matters? It sounds tiny. Is it only because of the threshold flips, or is there another reason to care about differences that small?
Only the threshold. The score of 0.5 is where decisions happen, and 0.7 percent of inputs sit close enough to it to flip. If nothing sat near the line I would have stopped caring.
Same trap going to a phone. Our TFLite conversion gave different results until we matched the epsilon, and nobody had mentioned it in the conversion notes.
Do you have a script that compares layer by layer? Diffing outputs only at the end hides where the error starts. Forward hooks on both sides and one tolerance per layer find it in minutes.

Yes. Hooks on the PyTorch side, and for Keras I save intermediate outputs with a second model that exposes them. np.allclose with atol 1e-4 per layer, printed as a table. It pointed at the first stride 2 conv immediately.

Backend view: any time two implementations should match, keep a golden set of a few hundred inputs with expected outputs in the repo and fail CI if more than a few flip. Cheap, and it catches this class of drift.
Both models in eval mode when you compared? I once compared Keras inference with PyTorch still in train mode, BatchNorm used batch statistics, and I lost a full afternoon.
Which side did you pad on, bottom and right or top and left? It depends on whether the input size is odd, so if your inputs vary in size the fix has to follow the size, not a fixed padding.

body: Added a CI step that posts screenshots of our five main screens at 360 px width on every pull request. On day one it showed a clipped button in the Yoruba version: the translated label was a third longer than the English one and the button text wrapped out of its box. Nobody had opened the Yoruba build on a small screen. Cheap step, and it paid for itself in a day.

comments.body: How much time does the screenshot step add to the pipeline? And are the screenshots kept for every build, or only the last one?

title: Offline bookmarks and reading position sync for a React Native news app
body:
React Native app for local publishers, used on weak signal and often offline. Readers save articles, bookmark them and keep a reading position, on a phone and sometimes a tablet. The backend is a Rust API in a Docker container with Postgres. I need sync that survives hours offline and two devices editing.

Options: last write wins per field with timestamps, simplest but phone clocks are wrong more often than I would like; an append-only change log per user with a cursor that the client replays; or CRDTs for the bookmark set, probably overkill for this data. I lean towards the change log. What would you pick, and how do you deal with device clocks?

comments.body: Change log with a per-user cursor, and let the server assign the order, not the device. Then device clocks do not matter. Bookmarks as add and remove operations on a set, last operation by server order wins. A CRDT would not give you more here.

From the design side: show a small state on each item, saved on this device or synced. When the status is unclear people tap the bookmark again and again, and with add and remove operations that can undo what they wanted.

body: Two changes this week for the Flutter app aimed at 2 GB phones. Building with split per ABI cut the download from 24 MB to 9 MB, and turning on icon tree shaking removed another 1.1 MB. Separately, the list endpoint returned 40 fields per row and the app used 9, so a select list in the query took the response from 310 KB to 62 KB. The second change helped more people than the first.

comments.body: If you publish an app bundle the store does the ABI split for you. Is the 9 MB figure from the store download or from the split APKs you build yourself?
Bundles handle it, yes. Per ABI APKs matter when you share the file outside the store, which happens a lot with apps passed between phones. Both numbers are useful.
For the 9 fields: did you make a separate endpoint or let the client name the fields? Field selection through a query parameter looks nice and gets messy once people ask for nested things.

title: Product grid jumps while images load on a Vue storefront
body: Vue storefront, product grid with loading lazy on the images. It works, but the grid jumps as images arrive because their height is unknown until then, which is bad on a cheap phone where it happens slowly. Images come in mixed ratios (square, 4:5, some landscape). Should I set aspect-ratio in CSS, store width and height in the product data and put them on the img tag, or force one ratio with object-fit and crop? The crop feels wrong for shoes.

title: ledgerround 1.1: invoice lines that add up to the total
body: ledgerround 1.1 is out. A small Python library that rounds invoice lines so they add up to the invoice total, using the largest remainder method, with Decimal throughout. Changes in 1.1: an allocate function that splits an amount by weights without losing a unit, per-line tax rounding modes, a local Decimal context so it no longer touches global settings, and a published file of input and expected output cases that ports must pass. Still rough: currencies with three decimals only work if you pass the exponent yourself, and the Java port that someone started is not finished.

comments.body: Could allocate be used to split one electricity bill across five sub-meters by consumption? Some readings come late, so the weights change after the first split.
Yes, weights can be anything non-negative, such as consumption in kWh as integers. If readings arrive late, rerun the allocation for the whole period, do not adjust the earlier result.
Is there a JavaScript version? The total in our checkout is computed in the browser and has to match the server to the last unit.
I would not compute it in both places. The server returns the lines and the total, and the browser only displays them. Two implementations drift, sooner or later.
Is the tie-break deterministic? When two lines have the same remainder, which one gets the extra unit? I need the same split on every run for reproducibility.
How does it handle tax-inclusive prices? Backing the tax out of a gross price rounds differently from adding it to a net one, and wholesalers ask for both.
A property check in CI would be a good addition: for random weights and totals, the parts always sum to the total. Hypothesis does this in a few lines and would catch edge cases like zeros.

Sometimes the browser has to show a live total before the server answers, like a point of sale that works offline. Then you need the same rule on both sides. A shared file of cases is how you keep them honest.

Not yet. I would rather publish a file of inputs and expected outputs that every port has to pass than maintain a second code base myself. If someone writes the JavaScript version, that file is the spec.

Design note: when the lines on an invoice are rounded so they sum, one of them can look wrong by a unit. A small line saying amounts are rounded avoids support mails from people who add them up on a phone calculator.
Back out the tax from the gross price with one rounding: net is the rounded gross divided by one plus the rate, and tax is gross minus net. Never round both separately, then they always add up.
I ported the rounding to Dart in about 60 lines. The hard part was matching the tie-break, the main rule was easy. A file of cases would have saved me a day.
Does 1.1 still rely on the global Decimal context? I was bitten by another library setting the precision for the whole process, and my totals changed with no code change on my side.
Is it pure Python? I would like to use it inside an Android app through Chaquopy, and anything with a compiled extension would be a problem there.
Bug: allocate with all weights at zero and a total of 10 raises ZeroDivisionError. A clear message about the weights would help whoever hits it, since it is easy to trigger with an empty month.
Is there a one page document with a worked invoice, lines, tax and total, so designers can see where the extra unit lands? I would like to draw the invoice screen from it.
A file of cases is the right call. We keep our design tokens the same way, one source file and every platform checks itself against it. Ports then stay honest without any meetings.
You say three decimal currencies work only if the exponent is passed. Is that a hard limit, or just the default being two? Tunisian and Kuwaiti dinars come up with some of our clients.
In our Vue storefront I did the totals with plain numbers and got 0.1 plus 0.2 style errors. Moved to integer minor units. A JavaScript port with the same cases file would help me as well.
The explanation of the largest remainder method in the readme was clear. I used allocate to split 1,000 images into train, validation and holdout by weights without losing or duplicating one.
Good catch. 1.1 uses a local context through localcontext and does not touch the global one. I should say that more clearly in the readme, thanks.
For the meter case, store the raw readings and compute the split on demand. If you save the rounded shares and a late reading comes in, you end up adjusting numbers that were already sent to people.
The changelog lists breaking changes in their own section, which is the part I actually read before bumping a version. More libraries should do that.
Does it also say which Python versions are supported in each release? That is the line I look for first when updating.
For shared bills, showing each person how their share was worked out matters more than the algorithm. Even a small breakdown table cuts the arguments.

title: ILIKE search on 60k products at 280 ms: trigram, full text or a search service?
body: Vue storefront on a Postgres database with 60,000 products. Search by name uses ILIKE with percent signs on both sides and takes 280 ms, more in a busy minute. Options: a pg_trgm index, Postgres full text search, or a small search service like Meilisearch. We are three people and I would like to avoid another service, but typo tolerance matters for shoppers typing on small keyboards.

comments.body: A search service gives typo tolerance almost for free, and it runs fine in one small container. The price is one more thing that can be down or out of date. For three people I would still try Postgres first.
Trigram first. A GIN index with pg_trgm usually brings that ILIKE down to a few milliseconds and handles misspellings reasonably. No new service, one migration.
Trigram fixed the speed but ranking is odd: shoes and shoe do not rank the way I expect, and a short word matches too many things. Maybe I need stemming?

Combine them. A tsvector with an English configuration handles stemming (shoes and shoe), and trigram handles the typos. Search with full text first and fall back to trigram if you get fewer than a few results.
Count the sync job in the cost of a search service. Keeping the index in step with Postgres is where it usually breaks, and a stale index is worse than a slow search because nobody notices.
Is the name search the only slow thing? The category and price filters on 60,000 rows should be covered by an index on (category_id, price). Check the whole query plan before blaming the search.

Le bundle perd 18 Ko gzip et je n'ai plus de fichiers de locale à gérer. Seul regret : pas de « il y a 5 minutes » tout fait, mais Intl.RelativeTimeFormat existe maintenant et le fait très bien.

comments.body: Vérifie le support de Intl.RelativeTimeFormat sur les vieux iPhone et les navigateurs de téléphones d'entrée de gamme. Si ton public a des appareils anciens, il faut une valeur de repli, sinon le texte reste vide.
Pour les fuseaux, stocke tout en UTC en base et ne convertis qu'à l'affichage. J'ai vu un projet où les horaires étaient décalés d'une heure parce que la base contenait des heures locales.

Pour Abidjan c'est UTC+0 toute l'année, donc il n'y aura jamais de décalage visible. Le piège apparaît avec un public à Casablanca ou au Caire, où l'heure change. Mieux vaut avoir le bon réflexe dès maintenant.
Tu gardes un polyfill pour Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, ou tu t'en passes ? Sur nos téléphones d'entrée de gamme, je n'ai jamais osé retirer les polyfills sans regarder les statistiques de navigateurs.
